title: Houses of Bala, Chetan, Divya (Atul's grid walk)

questions.prompt: Why do all the kids' endpoint positions lie on one single straight line?

options.text: They all repeat the same step

questions.explanation: Step 1: Each kid follows the same walking pattern — for example, "right 2, up 1" repeated. Step 2: When the same pattern is repeated from the same start (origin), every endpoint is a scaled-up version of the base step. Step 3: Scaled-up versions of one vector all lie on one line. Step 4: This "repeated step → straight line of endpoints" is the geometric meaning of *homogeneity* — and we will see it again as the *span of a vector* in Mission 3.

questions.prompt: As a kid takes more and more steps following the same pattern, the endpoint moves in which direction on the grid?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Each repeated step adds both a rightward and an upward move. Step 2: So every new endpoint is further right *and* further up than the previous one. Step 3: That combined motion traces a diagonal path outward from origin. Step 4: The trap "only horizontally right" would mean each step has no upward component — which contradicts the "up 1" part of the pattern. Step 5: This "diagonal outward" picture is the seed of *eigenvector direction* — a special direction along which a matrix scales without rotating, which we will study in Mission 13.

questions.prompt: What does it *mean* on the grid when two different kids end up at the same position?

options.text: They took no steps at all

questions.explanation: Step 1: A position is described by the pair (right-steps, up-steps) taken so far. Step 2: Two kids end at the same position iff their (right-steps, up-steps) totals are equal. Step 3: Different sequences can produce the same totals — that's the *commutativity* of grid moves. Step 4: The trap "no steps at all" describes the special case where both end at origin. Step 5: This "different paths, same endpoint" is the geometric meaning of *commutativity* — formally A · B = B · A, which we will study for matrices in Mission 7.

questions.prompt: If a kid turns left and then immediately turns right (with same step size), the net effect on direction is:
questions.explanation: Step 1: A "left" turn followed by an equal "right" turn cancels out. Step 2: The kid ends up facing the same direction they started. Step 3: This is true for any sequence where the turns sum to zero. Step 4: The trap "rotated left by twice" treats each turn as accumulating, not cancelling. Step 5: This "opposites cancel" property is the seed of *inverse operations* — a left turn is the *inverse* of a right turn, the same idea we will formalise for matrices in Mission 8.

questions.prompt: Why does walking the same pattern from origin always land on the same straight line of points?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Each step adds the same (right, up) shift — say (2, 1). Step 2: Adding the same shift repeatedly traces a straight diagonal line. Step 3: The endpoints are origin + n × (2, 1) for n = 0, 1, 2, … Step 4: This is the geometric picture of a *span* — the set of all "scaled copies" of one vector. Step 5: We will formalise this as *span{v}* in Mission 3 — the line generated by a single direction vector.

questions.prompt: If a kid walks "right 4, up 2" repeatedly from origin, the endpoints form what shape?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Each step adds the same shift (4, 2). Step 2: Repeating it produces points (0, 0), (4, 2), (8, 4), (12, 6) — all collinear. Step 3: The trap "circle" would require equal-distance points from origin — not the case here. Step 4: The trap "zigzag" would require alternating directions. Step 5: This "single direction → single line" geometry is the foundation of *one-dimensional subspaces*, the simplest case of *subspaces* in Mission 3.

questions.prompt: What stays *invariant* when a kid repeats the same walking pattern over and over?

options.text: The total steps taken each time

questions.explanation: Step 1: The *direction* of each step is fixed — same right-component, same up-component. Step 2: The endpoint *position* changes (it grows), and the *total steps* changes. Step 3: But the *direction* — the ratio of right to up — stays the same. Step 4: The trap "starting grid square" describes origin, which is also fixed, but origin is a *position*, not an *invariant*. Step 5: This "fixed direction under scaling" is the geometric meaning of *eigenvector*, which we will define formally in Mission 13.

questions.prompt: Why do repeated endpoints lie on a straight line and not a curve?
questions.explanation: Step 1: A straight step (right + up) is itself a straight line — no bend. Step 2: Repeating straight steps traces a longer straight line. Step 3: Curves appear only when steps bend or rotate. Step 4: The trap "endpoints zigzag corners" would be true for "right then left then right" — alternating direction. Step 5: This "straight + straight = straight" additivity is the seed of *linearity* — straight motions compose into straight motions, the property of *linear maps* we will use in Mission 12.

questions.prompt: If one kid walks the pattern longer than another kid, what changes about their final endpoint?

options.text: It sits at the same spot

questions.explanation: Step 1: Each step moves the endpoint outward by the same shift. Step 2: More steps means more shifts added — the endpoint moves further from origin. Step 3: The *direction* stays the same (same line), only the *distance* changes. Step 4: The trap "closer to origin" would mean steps shrink, but they don't. Step 5: This "scale by number of steps" idea is *scalar multiplication* — multiplying a vector by a number scales its length but not its direction. We will formalise this in Mission 3.

questions.prompt: How can a child predict the next endpoint without actually walking the next step?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The endpoints lie on a known line (drawn on the grid). Step 2: To predict the next endpoint, extend the line one more step in the same direction. Step 3: This is "extrapolation" — using the pattern to extend into the future. Step 4: The trap "add a fixed number" ignores which direction the line goes. Step 5: This is the essence of *linear prediction* — knowing the line tells you every future point, the basis of *regression* in statistics and *interpolation* in numerical methods.

questions.prompt: Why is "right 3, up 2" different from "up 2, right 3" in *outcome*, even though the kid ends at the same spot?
questions.explanation: Step 1: The two orders trace different routes — one goes east then north, the other north then east. Step 2: The endpoint is the same (because the moves commute). Step 3: But the *intermediate path* differs. Step 4: For kids this is obvious; for matrices, it is the famous A · B = B · A question. Step 5: When matrices *do* commute, they have a special property; when they don't, order matters. We will explore *commuting matrices* in Mission 12.

questions.prompt: If a kid walks partway through a pattern and then stops, what is left on the graph?

options.text: A partial step on the line

questions.explanation: Step 1: Stopping mid-pattern means the endpoint is only partway along the line. Step 2: The endpoint sits on the line between origin and the next full step. Step 3: No new line is created — just one point on the existing line. Step 4: This "intermediate endpoint lies on the same line" property is *convexity* — the line between any two points on a line is also on the line. Step 5: We will use this *convex combination* idea when discussing *subspaces* in Mission 3.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for several endpoints to "lie on one line"?
questions.explanation: Step 1: "Lie on one line" means a single straight line passes through every endpoint. Step 2: For endpoints of repeated same-step walks, they share one direction — the step direction. Step 3: The trap "form a circle" describes equidistant points, not collinear. Step 4: This "shared direction = collinear" is the geometric meaning of *linear dependence*, which we will formalise for arbitrary vectors in Mission 3.

questions.prompt: Why do different kids' endpoints align on the same line when they all walk the same pattern?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Same pattern → same direction of motion. Step 2: Starting from origin, every kid's endpoints are scalar multiples of the same step. Step 3: Scalar multiples of one vector all lie on one line through origin. Step 4: The trap "different shapes" describes different patterns, not the same one. Step 5: This "all scalar multiples of one vector lie on one line" is the formal definition of *one-dimensional subspace*, which we will study in Mission 3.

questions.prompt: If a kid takes a step "left 2, down 1" instead of "right 2, up 1", how does the line change?
questions.explanation: Step 1: "Left 2, down 1" is the negative of "right 2, up 1" — opposite direction. Step 2: So the line flips to the opposite diagonal — into the bottom-left quadrant. Step 3: The trap "stays exactly the same" ignores the sign change. Step 4: This "negation flips direction" property is *scalar multiplication by −1*, which we will use when defining *vector negation* in Mission 3.

questions.prompt: How is walking on a grid similar to reading a graph?
questions.explanation: Step 1: A grid walk produces a sequence of (x, y) positions. Step 2: A graph plots (x, y) positions on a sheet. Step 3: Both rely on the same coordinate system. Step 4: The trap "traces circles only" describes specific circular walks, not the general structure. Step 5: This "grid walk = graph plot" link is the seed of *parameterised curves* — describing a moving point by its coordinates over time. We will use this idea in Mission 14 when we study *eigen-decompositions*.

questions.prompt: If the same kid walks two different patterns (say one "right 2, up 1" and one "right 1, up 2"), how many different lines appear?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Pattern 1 gives endpoints along line 1; pattern 2 gives endpoints along line 2. Step 2: Different step directions give different lines. Step 3: The two lines both pass through origin but head in different directions. Step 4: This "two different directions → two different lines through origin" is the geometric meaning of *two linearly independent vectors* — a concept we will formalise in Mission 3 and use throughout the rest of the course.

questions.prompt: What if the same kid walked the same pattern but started from position (5, 3) instead of origin — how would the line change?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Starting from a new point shifts every endpoint by the same (5, 3) amount. Step 2: The shape stays a straight line, just translated. Step 3: The line is now *parallel* to the original but no longer passes through origin. Step 4: The trap "stays at origin" ignores the new starting position. Step 5: This "translated line is parallel to original" is the geometric meaning of *affine subspaces*, contrasted with *linear subspaces* — a distinction we will make formal in Mission 4.

questions.prompt: Why is a grid helpful for understanding lines and patterns?

options.text: It shows motion step by step

questions.explanation: Step 1: A grid makes each step visible — you can see the kid's position after every move. Step 2: This makes it easy to count and verify the endpoint formula. Step 3: The trap "hides all the steps" describes the opposite — a graph without gridlines. Step 4: This "step-by-step visualisation" is the same idea as *discretisation* — turning a smooth line into discrete sample points, the foundation of *numerical analysis*.

questions.prompt: What if a kid walked in a circle on the grid (right, up, left, down repeatedly) — what shape would the endpoints trace?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: "Right, up, left, down" returns to the starting position after four steps. Step 2: Repeating this trace a closed loop — same four endpoints every cycle. Step 3: This is *periodic motion* — a closed orbit. Step 4: The trap "straight line outward" describes unidirectional stepping, not circular. Step 5: This *periodic orbit* picture is the seed of *circles, ellipses, and eigen-rotations* — concepts that show up in *singular value decomposition* (Mission 14) and *Fourier analysis*.
